title: A Blueprint for Public Engagement Appraisal: Supporting Research Careers
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that public engagement work is undervalued in research institutions and is therefore poorly supported in researchers’ careers. The authors argue that outreach and public engagement are treated as optional, time-consuming activities rather than as legitimate work contributing to promotion, pay, and professional recognition.

To address this, the paper proposes a goal-setting and appraisal framework for public engagement built around supervision, periodic evaluation, and portfolio building. Researchers would meet with a supervisor to set values, goals, and actions, conduct interim reviews, and complete summative evaluations after each engagement activity. The evaluations would emphasize simple, practical indicators and narrative reflection rather than difficult-to-measure “impact” metrics.

The paper is framed around research institutions rather than a school-based intervention. Its examples and case study describe a postdoctoral researcher carrying out outreach talks for school audiences, but these are illustrative rather than empirical data. The broader context is institutional career development for public engagement across research settings.

The authors conclude that formal evaluation and portfolio-based recognition could encourage more researchers to engage with the public without forcing participation or creating excessive administrative burden. They recommend that institutions implement evaluation systems, support public engagement through supervision and training, and use appraisals as part of career advancement decisions.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/advocacy paper proposing a public engagement appraisal framework, not an empirical evaluation study. It contains no experimental or observational methodology assessing educational outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measured impact on K-12 science outcomes or any intervention effect sizes. It is policy-oriented and only discusses potential benefits hypothetically.
